# Prescriptive lessons -- benson x method-vol-7-blues-ideas

## dom7

Benson treats the dominant-7th chord as a layered construction site, not a single-scale situation. The foundational move is always Blues Scale first, then modal hybrids, then maj7 superimposition -- each layer added on top of, not instead of, the one before. At the structural level, harmonic-region thinking (not voice-leading proximity alone) licenses chord swaps, with tempo as one explicit filter: the Fmaj7 interchangeable substitution favors faster contexts.

- [ch.4 p.17] Even when two scales share enharmonically identical pitch content, they must be mentally pictured as distinct depending on dominant-chord context -- G Major Phrygian and C Harmonic Minor are the same pitches but require separate visualization.
- [ch.4 p.21] Do not become a "parrot" by memorizing lines without internalizing their harmonic concept; the lines are vehicles for understanding, not ends in themselves.
- [ch.4 p.21] Do not study the whole blues form at once -- each section and each harmonic possibility must be isolated and mastered before assembling the full form.
- [ch.6 p.27] Over a D7(9) dominant vamp, begin with Blues Scale ideas as the foundational layer before adding modal or superimposition vocabulary. Blues Scale is the first of three escalating technique categories, not an option to be skipped.
- [ch.6 p.31] Over D7(9), layer Mixolydian, Lydian Dominant, and Blues ideas simultaneously as a single combined approach -- not sequentially or in isolation.
- [ch.6 p.35] Over D7(9) or any dominant-7th vamp, superimpose major-7th arpeggios while simultaneously drawing on Blues Scale, Mixolydian, and Lydian Dominant; this three-layer blend is the most advanced static dominant technique in the book.
- [ch.7 p.38] The Fmaj7 interchangeable-chord substitution works better at faster tempos -- one of the book's few explicitly tempo-conditioned substitution rules. At slower tempos it should not be the first-choice option.
- [ch.7 p.40] Over any dominant-7th chord, any chord from the same Harmonic Region may be substituted as an "Interchangeable Chord Trick"; the regional relationship -- not voice-leading proximity alone -- licenses the swap.
- [ch.9 p.53] When the V degree of a superimposed cadence is itself a tritone substitution of a real dominant, expand available scale colors beyond Dorian to include Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished.
- [ch.10 p.62] Bm7 Dorian substituting for F7 produces a combination sound between F Dominant Diminished and F Altered Scale, leading naturally toward Bb7.
- [ch.10 p.72] The cadence Ebm7/Ab7 replacing D7 permits Ab7 Lydian Dominant or Ab7 Dominant Diminished because Ab7 is the tritone substitute of D7; alternatively, collapse the cadence to a single Ebm7 Dorian or hybrid.
- [ch.12 p.98] During the turnaround bars (last two bars of the blues form), rest rather than play melodic ideas -- use silence to phrase-separate choruses and create breathing space between melodic "stories." The book explicitly declines to focus on melodic possibilities for the turnaround; it is breathing space, not a soloing opportunity.

## dom7b9

Over altered dominants, Benson's characteristic macro-move is substitution by harmonic region rather than chord-to-chord exchange: derive replacement chords by tracing the parallel minor of the subdominant, then its relative majors and minor-subdominant-region members. The method stacks multiple derivation paths (tritone substitution, subdominant minor region, leading-tone diminished) as parallel options for the same target chord.

- [ch.8 p.44] Over D7(#9) or any altered dominant, the IV-degree chord (e.g., C7) may be replaced by its tritone substitute (F#7 or Gb7), crossing into an adjacent dominant region.
- [ch.8 p.46] Over Bb7 functioning as the subdominant in F, substitute Gbmaj7 derived from the Subdominant Minor region: the derivation path is parallel minor of the subdominant (Bbm) -- its relative chords -- yielding Gbmaj7.
- [ch.8 p.50] Emaj7 can replace Bb7 by extending minor-tonality subdominant region rules into major tonalities: treat the home key's parallel minor (Fm), find its relative major (Ab), and extract Minor Subdominant Region chords from Ab -- yielding Emaj7. This is the book's densest substitution derivation.
- [ch.8 p.52] Bm7 (a Minor Subdominant Region chord) may replace Bb7 (a Major Subdominant Region chord) over an altered dominant context, applying regional interchangeability across subdominant region types.

## maj7

Benson consistently assigns Lydian -- not the diatonic mode of the home key -- to any non-diatonic major-7th substitution chord, because Lydian over that chord simultaneously exposes the altered tensions of the target dominant. Major-7th chords also function as superimposition objects over dominant contexts, and as color sources within superimposed IIm7-I cadences via relative-chord relationships.

- [ch.6 p.35] Superimpose major-7th arpeggios over dominant-7th chord contexts, combining them with Blues Scale, Mixolydian, and Lydian Dominant vocabulary simultaneously; this is the top layer of the three-layer static dominant technique.
- [ch.9 p.53] In superimposed IIm7-I cadences, the relative major of the IIm7 (i.e., the IV -- e.g., Fmaj7 relative to Dm7) and the relative minor of the Imaj7 (e.g., Am7 relative to Cmaj7) are always available as additional color sources.
- [ch.10 p.60] Any non-diatonic major-7th substitution chord must be treated as Lydian; Lydian over Bmaj7 simultaneously reveals the altered tensions of the target F7 (#9, b9, #11, b13). The note Bb (A#) -- major 7th of B and perfect 4th of F -- functions as a special dual-role color note giving the substitution its distinctive flavor.

## min7

Over non-diatonic minor-7th substitution chords, Benson's consistent prescription is Dorian as the scale identity (never the home-key diatonic mode), and hybrid ideas -- Dorian blended with altered tensions from the target dominant -- as the preferred sound over strict modal application. The V degree of any superimposed IIm7-V7-I cadence is to be stripped: it loses tension-bearing capacity and collapses back into the IIm7 Dorian, leaving only IIm7 and Imaj7 as active functional identities. Color notes -- pitches functioning simultaneously at two interval roles -- are identified as the primary flavor generators and foregrounded in melodic lines.

- [ch.9 p.53] Apply Dorian ideas over the IIm7 degree and Lydian ideas over its relative IV chord in superimposed cadences (e.g., in C major: Dorian over Dm7, Lydian over Fmaj7).
- [ch.9 p.53] Do not apply strict diatonic modal thinking over non-diatonic minor-7th substitution chords; hybrid ideas (Dorian combined with altered dominant color) tend to sound better than pure modal application. This aesthetic prescription is stated explicitly: "Usually hybrid ideas tend to sound better."
- [ch.9 p.53] When superimposing a IIm7-V7-I cadence, do not apply leading dominant-7th scale tensions over the V degree -- the V loses tension-bearing capacity under superimposition and becomes part of the IIm7 Dorian.
- [ch.10 p.62] Any non-diatonic minor-7th substitution chord (e.g., Bm7 replacing F7) must be treated as Dorian -- not as a diatonic mode of the home key -- because it does not belong to the home key's chord family.
- [ch.10 p.69] When a IIm7-V7-I cadence is superimposed over a dominant chord, strip the V7 degree; only IIm7 and Imaj7 remain as active functional identities.
- [ch.10 p.70] A hybrid aesthetic preference is stated again: Dorian or hybrid ideas over each member of a consecutive minor-7th substitution chain tend to sound better than strict modal application.
- [ch.10 p.70] A stepwise chain of consecutive minor-7th chords (e.g., Bbm7-Am7-G#m7) may substitute for a single dominant target; play Dorian or hybrid ideas over each member. G#m7 Dorian over D7 simultaneously produces a combination of D Altered and D Dominant Diminished sound.
- [ch.11 p.95] The cadence Ebm7/Ab7 replacing Bb7 should be treated as a single Ebm7 Dorian or Ebm7 hybrid derived from the Minor Subdominant Region (Bbm -- Gbmaj7 -- its relative Ebm7) of the home key.
- [ch.12 p.100] Cm7/F7 may replace A half-diminished because Ao is an inversion of Cm6, which equals F7(9); further, Cm7 Dorian and Ao Locrian share the same notes as both derive from the Bb key. Treat as a single Cm7 Dorian identity.
- [ch.12 p.110] C#m7/F#7 substituting for C7 should be read as a single C#m7 Dorian, which produces altered tensions (#9, b9, #11, b13) against C7; the note B (minor 7th of C#m, major 7th of C) is the primary color note.
- [ch.12 p.115] Reading the C#m7/F#7-C7 cadence as a single F#m7 Dorian or F#m7 hybrid produces a sound combining C7 Dominant Diminished with C7alt; B is again the pivotal color note.
- [ch.12 p.120] When a minor-7th substitution chord contains a note functioning simultaneously at two interval roles, identify those dual-function pitches as primary flavor generators and foreground them in the melodic line.

## dim7

Benson uses diminished chords exclusively as V7 surrogates, licensed by the leading-tone principle: the chord's notes lie a half step above the tones of the target dominant. The method extends the leading-tone concept beyond the half step (a whole step can also function as a leading tone), and traces specific diminished-chord identities back to their subdominant-region or dominant-region targets.

- [ch.8 p.49] Diminished chords built on the root function as V7 substitutes because their notes lie a half step above the notes of the target dominant, creating multiple simultaneous leading tones.
- [ch.10 p.63] The leading-tone principle extends beyond the half step: a note may function as a leading tone even if it is a whole step from its resolution target.
- [ch.10 p.63] Bo (= Fo = E7 with different bass) substitutes for the Subdominant Region chord Bb7 by functioning as C7 (Dominant Region chord) leading to Fmaj7; all notes of E7 (except the flat 7th) lie a half step from Fmaj7 tones.

## min7b5

Half-diminished chords are treated as harmonically equivalent to specific minor-7th/dominant-7th cadences and collapsed into a single Dorian identity for improvisation purposes. The equivalence is derived from inversion and enharmonic reasoning, not voice-leading convention.

- [ch.12 p.100] A half-diminished chord (e.g., Ao) may be replaced by a Cm7/F7 cadence collapsed into a single Cm7 Dorian identity, because Ao is an inversion of Cm6 = F7(9), and Cm7 Dorian and Ao Locrian share the same notes as both derive from the Bb key.
